items.title: The Case for Productive Struggle
items.passage:
For generations, good teaching was easy to recognize: a knowledgeable instructor delivered clear explanations while students listened and took notes. Clarity still matters, but research on learning has gradually shifted attention from what students hear to what they do. A growing number of educators now argue that the most durable learning often begins where understanding breaks down.

The idea is usually described as productive struggle. When learners wrestle with a problem before being shown the solution, they must retrieve what they already know, notice gaps, and build connections between ideas. These mental operations feel effortful, and the effort is precisely the point. Material that arrives too smoothly can create a pleasant illusion of competence that fades quickly once the lesson ends.

This does not mean abandoning guidance. Novices can flounder when a task is too open-ended, and frustration that turns into hopelessness teaches nothing. The art lies in calibration: problems should sit just beyond what students can currently manage alone, yet within reach with hints, peer discussion, or a well-timed question. Teachers therefore need to resist the urge to rescue learners at the first sign of difficulty.

Assessment practices complicate matters. Grades tend to reward quick correct answers, which encourages students to hide confusion rather than explore it. Some schools now separate the grade for a final product from the feedback given during practice, so that mistakes made while rehearsing carry no penalty. The aim is to make experimentation feel safe.

None of this is an argument for making school needlessly hard. Struggle is productive only when it is purposeful, when learners understand why a task is worth the discomfort, and when they receive feedback soon enough to adjust. Encouraged in that way, students may leave school not merely with facts in hand but with the confidence to approach unfamiliar problems.

questions.q: What shift in emphasis does the author describe in the first paragraph?
options: From clear explanations to the notes students take during lessons
From what students hear to what students actually do
From difficult problems to easy classroom exercises
From teacher training to the design of examination papers
questions.explain: 第一段明确指出研究重心已从“学生听到什么”转向“学生做什么”，故选第二项。第一项仍停留在听讲层面，第三、四项文中均未提及。

questions.q: The phrase "a pleasant illusion of competence" in paragraph 2 refers to
options: learners overestimating how much they have learned because the material came easily
teachers believing that their explanations are more effective than they are
the confidence that grows from solving a genuinely difficult problem
the satisfaction students feel when they receive timely feedback
questions.explain: 该短语承接上文“材料来得太顺”，指学生因学习过程毫不费力而高估自己的掌握程度。第二项偷换主体，第三项与“困难才有价值”的论点相反，第四项在文中指反馈，与错觉无关。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, why can excessive frustration be harmful?
options: It makes students dislike the subject for a long time
It takes too much class time away from explanations
It can turn into hopelessness, which teaches nothing
It forces teachers to provide fewer hints than usual
questions.explain: 第三段说明当挫败感变成绝望时就什么也教不会，故第三项正确。第一项文中未提“长期厌恶”，第二项讨论的是课堂时间，第四项与“给予提示”的建议不符。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about conventional grading in paragraph 4?
options: Marks should be abolished entirely in secondary schools
Grades can discourage students from revealing their confusion
Feedback during practice is less valuable than a final mark
Students always perform better when marks are removed
questions.explain: 第四段指出评分倾向于奖励快速正确的答案，从而促使学生掩饰困惑而非探索困惑。第一项过度推断，第三项与文中“把反馈与终评分开”的做法相反，第四项表述绝对。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph about productive struggle?
options: It suits advanced learners far better than beginners
It should be applied to every task regardless of difficulty
It matters more than the quality of the teacher's explanations
Its benefits depend on purpose and on timely feedback
questions.explain: 末段强调只有具备目的性并及时获得反馈时，挣扎才是有益的，故第四项正确。第一项无依据，第二项与“不必刻意为难学生”矛盾，第三项比较两者重要性，文中并未如此断言。

items.title: The Cost of Frictionless Technology
items.passage:
Modern digital tools are designed to remove friction. Maps calculate routes, keyboards correct our spelling, and platforms decide which films we might enjoy. Each small convenience is genuinely welcome, and few users would willingly return to a world of paper maps and manual indexes. Yet the smoothness of these systems invites a question that designers rarely address: what happens to the abilities we stop using?

Skills tend to fade when they are never exercised. Someone who always follows a navigation prompt may gradually lose the habit of building a mental map of a city, and a student who leans on automatic correction may become less certain about spelling without assistance. This is not nostalgia for older tools. It is a familiar pattern: competence that is outsourced to a device tends to remain undeveloped or quietly decline.

The effects are uneven. A tool that handles routine work can free attention for more demanding tasks, and few people would argue that mental arithmetic should compete with a spreadsheet. The concern arises when reliance becomes invisible. When people can no longer notice that a decision has been made for them, or explain why a recommendation appeared, they lose the ability to question the system and to correct it when it fails.

Designers have begun to respond with tools that invite engagement rather than replace it. Some navigation applications, for instance, offer a broader view before zooming in, so users still form a rough sense of direction. Others explain the reason behind a suggestion. The common principle is to leave the user with a role, however small, in the process.

What matters, then, is not whether we use intelligent tools but how we use them. Convenience is not a vice, and no one should be asked to perform every task unaided. But a useful test is to ask what a tool is doing for us and what it may be doing instead of us. Tools that keep that distinction visible are more likely to remain servants rather than substitutes.

questions.q: What does the author acknowledge about digital convenience in the first paragraph?
options: It is rarely welcomed by ordinary users
It is genuinely useful, and few people would give it up
It matters mainly to younger users
It has made all older tools worthless
questions.explain: 首段承认每种便利都“确实受欢迎”，且很少有人愿意回到纸质地图的时代，故选第二项。第一项与原文相反，第三项文中未提年龄差异，第四项用“all”过度绝对。

questions.q: The phrase "reliance becomes invisible" in paragraph 3 most nearly means that people
options: depend on tools without realizing how much is decided for them
cannot see the tools because they are installed in devices
stop caring whether the software is updated
refuse to use any automated system
questions.explain: 下文紧接说明人们察觉不到某个决定已由系统代做，也无法解释推荐从何而来，故指“不自觉地依赖”。第二项把比喻当成字面意思，第三项谈更新维护，第四项与整段内容相反。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, when does reliance on technology become a real concern?
options: When it takes over routine tasks such as calculation
When the devices involved become expensive to repair
When users cannot see the decisions made for them or explain recommendations
When designers keep adding new features to their products
questions.explain: 第三段把问题限定在依赖变得“不可见”之时，即用户无法察觉替代决策、无法解释推荐。第一项作者认为常规任务被接管反可释放注意力，第二、四项文中均未涉及。

questions.q: What do some designers do to encourage users to stay involved?
options: They remove explanations so that users must guess
They hide the purpose of the tool from its users
They withdraw all forms of assistance
They offer a broader view before zooming in and explain suggestions
questions.explain: 第四段举例说部分导航应用先给全景再放大，另有工具解释建议的理由，故第四项正确。第一、二项与“让过程可见”相反，第三项与“给用户留一个角色”矛盾。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Intelligent tools should be avoided wherever possible
Users ought to perform every task without any assistance
The value of a tool depends on whether users stay aware of its role
Convenience is a serious fault in modern design
questions.explain: 末段提出要分清工具“为我们做什么”和“代替我们做什么”，并让这种区分保持可见，故第三项正确。第一、二项过于极端，第四项与作者“便利并非恶习”的表述矛盾。

items.title: The Quiet Return of Repair
items.passage:
Not long ago, throwing away a broken object was a practical decision. A faulty kettle or a torn jacket often cost less to replace than to mend, and repair services were scarce in many neighborhoods. In recent years, however, a counter-movement has taken shape, driven less by nostalgia than by a simple calculation: the things we discard carry materials, energy, and labor that are expensive to replace.

Repair events and community workshops have appeared in many towns, where volunteers help visitors fix small appliances, bicycles, and clothing. Their appeal lies partly in money saved, but also in the experience itself. A person who opens a device and finds a loose connection learns that the object is not a mysterious sealed box. That shift in perception can change how people shop, and how long they keep what they buy.

Manufacturers influence this more than any campaign. Products that can be opened, that share standard parts, and that come with spare components are far easier to repair. Some companies have begun to publish manuals and sell parts, partly in response to consumer pressure, partly because durable products can build loyalty. The trend is uneven, and sealed designs remain common, but the direction of the conversation has changed.

Repair culture also raises awkward questions. Some fixes are genuinely risky, particularly when they involve electricity, gas, or safety equipment, and a well-meaning attempt can create a new hazard. There is also the matter of time: many people would rather buy a new item than spend an afternoon learning to mend an old one. Campaigns that ignore these realities tend to preach to the converted.

The most persuasive argument for repair may be the least dramatic. It is not that everyone should become a technician, but that keeping some objects in use should be an ordinary option rather than an unusual act. When spare parts, clear instructions, and skilled help are within reach, repair stops being a hobby for enthusiasts and becomes what it once was: a normal part of owning things.

questions.q: What reason does the author give for the growth of repair culture?
options: A widespread longing for the habits of an earlier age
New laws that require manufacturers to offer repairs
The high cost of the materials and energy contained in discarded goods
The growing difficulty of finding new products to buy
questions.explain: 首段指出这场运动更多出于“计算”而非怀旧：被丢弃的物品内含昂贵的材料、能源与劳动，故选第三项。第一项恰好被作者否定，第二、四项文中无据。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what is one effect of opening a device at a repair event?
options: People realize that objects are not sealed and mysterious after all
People are encouraged to buy replacements more often
People begin to doubt the skills of the volunteers
People conclude that every repair is simple and quick
questions.explain: 第二段说打开设备的人会发现物件并非神秘的黑箱，这种认知转变会影响购买习惯，故第一项正确。第二项与原文相反，第三项无据，第四项过度概括，文中也承认部分维修有风险。

questions.q: What role do manufacturers play according to the passage?
options: They have no real influence on how long products last
They have stopped producing sealed designs altogether
They sell parts only to professional repair shops
Their design choices largely determine how repairable a product is
questions.explain: 第三段明确说厂商比任何宣传都更有影响力：能否打开、是否通用零件、是否供应备件决定可修性，故第四项正确。第一项与原文相反，第二项被“密封设计仍常见”否定，第三项文中未提。

questions.q: The word "converted" in paragraph 4 most probably means people who
options: have changed their religious beliefs
are already convinced and need no persuasion
repair objects in exchange for payment
design products for large companies
questions.explain: “preach to the converted”指只对已经认同的人说教，故指“已被说服的人”。第一项是字面宗教义，此处为比喻；第三、四项与语境无关。

questions.q: What can be inferred about the author's view of repair?
options: Everyone should train to become a professional technician
Repair is a temporary fashion that will soon disappear
Repair should become an everyday option supported by parts and guidance
Repair is too dangerous to be encouraged at all
questions.explain: 末段提出维修应成为普通选项，前提是备件、说明与熟练帮助触手可及，故第三项正确。第一项被“不必人人成为技师”否定，第二项与全文趋势相反，第四项夸大了第四段对风险的提醒。

items.title: The Hidden Cost of Sitting Still
items.passage:
For most of human history, physical activity was not something people scheduled. It was built into the shape of daily life: walking to collect water, carrying firewood, working land. Modern routines are different. Many people can now pass an entire working day without standing for more than a few minutes, and the body was never designed for that kind of stillness.

The problem is not simply a lack of formal exercise. Someone may run in the morning and still spend most of the day seated, and researchers increasingly argue that long, uninterrupted sitting has effects of its own. Muscles that remain idle for hours process fuel differently, and the circulation of blood slows. These changes are subtle, which is exactly why they are easy to ignore.

The encouraging news is that small interruptions appear to matter. Getting up to fill a glass of water, taking a short walk during a phone call, or simply standing while reading can break up long periods of stillness. The goal is not a workout; it is to reset the body's pattern. Individuals who build such moments into their routines often report that the habit is easier to sustain than a formal exercise plan.

Workplaces shape this behavior more than willpower does. When stairs are more visible than lifts, when meetings are sometimes held on foot, and when short breaks are treated as normal rather than as laziness, movement becomes the path of least resistance. Culture matters too: employees who leave their desks may be judged as uncommitted unless the organization makes clear that it expects them to move.

None of this dismisses the value of planned exercise, which remains important for strength, endurance, and mood. But it does suggest that the question "Did I work out today?" is too narrow. How long we sit without interruption, and how readily our surroundings let us move, may matter as much as the hours we spend in a gym. The remedy is partly personal and partly collective.

questions.q: What does the author say about physical activity in the past?
options: It was something people deliberately scheduled each week
It was built into the ordinary pattern of daily life
It was rare because most work required little movement
It was mainly performed in dedicated exercise spaces
questions.explain: 首段说过去的体力活动并非刻意安排，而是融入日常：取水、搬柴、耕地，故选第二项。第一项与原文相反，第三项无据，第四项是现代健身房的模式而非过去。

questions.q: The word "subtle" in paragraph 2 most probably means
options: immediately visible to anyone
medically serious and painful
slight and easily overlooked
temporary and self-correcting
questions.explain: 下文说这些变化“正因为细微才容易被忽视”，故指“轻微而不易察觉”。第一项与“易被忽略”矛盾，第二项文中未提疼痛，第四项无依据。

questions.q: What are the small interruptions in paragraph 3 meant to do?
options: Break up long periods of inactivity
Replace a formal exercise plan completely
Build strength and muscle quickly
Increase the length of the working day
questions.explain: 第三段说明这些小动作的目的是“打断长时间的静止”，而非进行锻炼，故选第一项。第二项与“目标不是锻炼”不符，第三项属于有计划的运动，第四项文中未提。

questions.q: In the author's view, what largely shapes whether people move at work?
options: The strength of individual willpower
The length of the working day
Personal fitness levels before employment
Whether the environment and the culture make movement easy and accepted
questions.explain: 第四段开头即说工作场所对行为的影响大于意志力，并列举楼梯可见、步行开会、不把短休视为偷懒等，故第四项正确。第一项被原文直接否定，第二、三项文中未论及。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Gym exercise is no longer necessary for healthy adults
The arrangement of furniture and stairs is irrelevant
Reducing uninterrupted sitting deserves attention alongside planned exercise
Only employers are able to solve the problem
questions.explain: 末段说“今天锻炼了吗”这一问题太狭窄，久坐时长的意义可能不亚于健身时间，故第三项正确。第一项与“计划性运动仍重要”矛盾，第二项与全文相反，第四项忽略了文中“部分靠个人”的表述。

items.title: Rethinking the Working Week
items.passage:
The idea of a shorter working week has moved from the margins of debate into ordinary conversation. Advocates argue that many office jobs contain hours of low-value activity, and that compressing the week could sharpen focus. Critics reply that the notion is unrealistic for hospitals, factories, and shops, where work must be done at particular times. Both sides have a point, which is why the discussion is more interesting than it first appears.

Much of the evidence about shorter schedules comes from workplaces that chose to experiment, so conclusions should be drawn carefully. A team that volunteers for a trial is not a typical sample, and the enthusiasm of a new arrangement can fade after the novelty passes. Even so, the basic lesson seems durable: when hours are shorter, people tend to protect them. Meetings shrink, interruptions are tolerated less readily, and work that once expanded to fill the day is completed in less time.

The arrangement suits some jobs far better than others. Knowledge work, which depends on concentration and creativity, may gain from a tight schedule. Care work, sales, and emergency services are different: coverage matters more than efficiency, and a shorter week usually means hiring more people rather than working differently. In those settings, the real question is not hours but staffing and pay.

There is also a fairness issue. If shorter weeks become a privilege of certain occupations, the gap between secure office jobs and shift work may widen. A serious policy would need to consider who bears the costs of change. Some experiments reduce hours without cutting pay, which is generous but hard to sustain across an entire economy. Others cut pay as well, which tends to be unpopular.

Perhaps the most useful outcome of the debate is not a fixed answer but a better question: which parts of the working day are genuinely productive, and which parts exist out of habit? Organizations that answer that honestly may find room for change even where a shortened week remains impractical.

questions.q: What is the critics' main objection to a shorter working week?
options: It would reduce pay for office employees
It is unrealistic where work must happen at set times
It would make employees less careful about quality
It suits hospitals but not other workplaces
questions.explain: 首段指出批评者认为对医院、工厂、商店而言不现实，因为这些地方的工作必须在特定时间完成，故选第二项。第一项是后文减薪方案的讨论，第三项无据，第四项把适用范围说反了。

questions.q: The word "durable" in paragraph 2 most nearly means
options: lasting and reliable
surprising and new
expensive to test
flexible in practice
questions.explain: 此处说即使样本有局限，“基本教训”似乎依然成立且持久，故为“经得起时间检验”。第一项最贴合；第二项与 novelty 的语境相反，第三、四项与语义无关。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what tends to happen when working hours are shortened?
options: Meetings multiply and take up more time
People become more protective of their time
Work expands to fill the shorter day
The quality of work falls sharply
questions.explain: 第二段说工时缩短后人们更倾向于守住时间：会议变短、更不容忍打断，故选第二项。第一、三项与原文相反，第四项文中未作此判断。

questions.q: Why does the author say the arrangement suits some jobs better than others?
options: Because knowledge workers refuse to work in teams
Because shift workers are paid more than office staff
Because in care work and emergency services, coverage matters more than efficiency
Because fewer people are needed in factories and shops
questions.explain: 第三段区分两类工作：知识型工作依赖专注与创造，而护理、销售、应急服务更看重覆盖，缩短工时往往需要增加人手，故选第三项。第一、二项文中无据，第四项与“需多招人”相反。

questions.q: What can be inferred about the author's attitude toward the debate?
options: The debate is largely meaningless because no answer is possible
Shorter weeks should be adopted everywhere at once
Office workers deserve privileges that others do not
The discussion is valuable because it clarifies which hours are truly productive
questions.explain: 末段说这场辩论最有价值的成果不是固定答案，而是更好的问题——哪些工时真正有产出，故第四项正确。第一项与作者“讨论很有意思”的态度相反，第二、三项都非作者主张。

items.title: Museums That Tell Stories
items.passage:
A museum is often imagined as a quiet hall of objects, each displayed behind glass. That image is not wrong, but it is incomplete. In practice, every exhibition makes choices: what to include, where to place it, and what to say about it. A single label can decide whether a visitor sees a pot as a technical achievement, a household tool, or a sign of trade with distant places.

In recent decades, many museums have become more openly storytelling institutions. Exhibitions are arranged to guide visitors through an argument, and digital guides, audio trails, and immersive rooms are used to provide context. The intention is generous: to make collections meaningful to people who arrive without specialist knowledge, and to show that objects were made and used by human beings.

Not everyone is persuaded. Some historians worry that a strong narrative can smooth over uncertainty, presenting as settled what is still debated. A story is easier to follow than a set of competing interpretations, and visitors may leave with confidence that experts do not share. Others argue that a museum should not pretend to be neutral, since its choices already express values.

The more interesting question is how to combine narrative with honesty. Curators who do it well make the process visible: they explain why an object matters, admit where evidence is thin, and show that collections themselves have histories, including the difficult ways in which some objects were acquired. Visitors respond well to this candor. Being trusted with complexity, it turns out, is more engaging than being told a tidy story.

Museums are not merely storehouses; they are places where a society decides what to remember and how to explain it to itself. That responsibility argues for imagination and care in equal measure. A good exhibition leaves visitors not with a finished message but with a question they did not have before they walked in.

questions.q: What does the author say about exhibition choices in the first paragraph?
options: They are neutral because museums avoid value judgments
Only the objects on display really matter
Decisions about inclusion and labels shape what visitors understand
Museums deliberately avoid explaining objects to visitors
questions.explain: 首段说每场展览都在做选择：展什么、放哪里、如何说明，一块标签就能决定观众如何理解一件器物，故选第三项。第一项与后文“选择本身已表达价值”矛盾，第二、四项与展签说明的例子相反。

questions.q: Why have many museums turned toward storytelling?
options: To attract specialist researchers rather than general visitors
To make collections meaningful to people without specialist knowledge
To reduce the cost of maintaining their buildings
To avoid taking any position on difficult subjects
questions.explain: 第二段明确说其用心是让没有专业背景的观众也能理解藏品，并展示器物由人制作和使用，故选第二项。第一项与“非专业观众”相反，第三项无据，第四项与后文“不必假装中立”相悖。

questions.q: The word "candor" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: a confident and forceful tone
careful avoidance of difficult topics
detailed visual decoration
frank honesty about what is known and unknown
questions.explain: 上文说策展人承认证据薄弱、说明藏品来历，下文说观众乐于被信任去面对复杂性，故指“坦率诚实”。第一项侧重语气，第二项与“承认薄弱”相反，第三项与语境无关。

questions.q: According to the author, how do visitors respond to complexity?
options: They engage with it when they are trusted to handle it
They prefer to be given a tidy message
They become confused and leave the museum
They reject any narrative offered by curators
questions.explain: 第四段末句说“被信任去面对复杂性，比被灌输一个整洁的故事更有吸引力”，故选第一项。第二项正是作者所否定的做法，第三项无据，第四项与观众“反响良好”相反。

questions.q: What can be inferred about a good exhibition from the last paragraph?
options: It answers every question a visitor might have
It avoids raising any question at all
It provokes new questions rather than delivering a finished message
It presents one settled interpretation of the past
questions.explain: 末段说好展览留给观众的不是完成的信息，而是一个此前没有的问题，故选第三项。第一、二项与“不是完成的信息”矛盾，第四项与全文倡导的诚实呈现分歧相反。

items.title: Science's Invisible Results
items.passage:
Scientific progress is usually described as a sequence of discoveries: a hypothesis is tested, a result is announced, and knowledge advances. This account is tidy but misleading. Most experiments do not produce a striking outcome, and many fail to support the idea that inspired them. Such results are essential, because they tell researchers which paths are worth abandoning, yet they are far less likely to be published or read.

The asymmetry has consequences. If journals prefer clear, positive findings, then the published record becomes a distorted sample of what was actually tried. Researchers may waste time repeating failures that were never reported, and readers may overestimate how consistent the evidence is. The problem is structural rather than a matter of individual dishonesty: careers depend on visible success, and invisible results do not build reputations.

Reformers have proposed several remedies. Some journals now accept studies on the basis of their methods, before the results are known, so that an unexciting outcome cannot be a reason for rejection. Others publish registered reports, in which the design is reviewed in advance, or offer formats devoted to negative results. Each approach has costs, particularly the extra work of reviewing a study twice.

Replication is the related issue. A single demonstration, however elegant, may reflect chance or an unnoticed factor. Confirmation by independent groups is what turns an interesting observation into a dependable one, but such work is often seen as unoriginal, and funding tends to favor novelty. The culture of science therefore rewards the very thing it claims to distrust: isolated, dramatic findings.

The deeper point concerns honesty about uncertainty. Science works not because its results are always right but because its errors can eventually be found. That requires a record that includes the failures as well as the successes. A field that publishes only its victories slowly loses the information it needs to test itself.

questions.q: What does the author say about the results of most experiments?
options: They are dramatic and immediately useful
They are never worth publishing at all
They are usually reported before they are checked
They are unremarkable or unsupportive of the original idea
questions.explain: 首段指出多数实验不会产生惊人结果，许多甚至不支持原来的设想，故选第四项。第一项与原文相反，第二项与“这些结果至关重要”矛盾，第三项讨论的是报道时机，文中未提。

questions.q: What does the author identify as the cause of the publication problem?
options: Structural incentives rather than individual dishonesty
Deliberate fraud committed by most researchers
A shortage of journals willing to publish results
A lack of public interest in scientific work
questions.explain: 第二段明确说问题在于结构性激励——职业发展依赖可见的成功，而非个人不诚实，故选第一项。第二项被原文直接排除，第三、四项文中未提及。

questions.q: The word "asymmetry" in paragraph 2 most probably refers to
options: disagreement among journals about standards
unequal funding between scientific fields
the gap between the work that is done and the work that is published
the balance between theory and experiment
questions.explain: 上文说大量未产生惊人结果的实验极少被发表，第二段随即讨论这种“做过的”与“发表的”之间的不对等，故选第三项。第一、二、四项均非该词所指。

questions.q: Why is replication described as being treated as unoriginal?
options: Because it always confirms earlier results
Because it is seen as unoriginal while funding favors novelty
Because it requires no funding at all
Because it is theoretically impossible to carry out
questions.explain: 第四段说重复验证常被视为缺乏新意，而经费更青睐新颖性，故选第二项。第一项与“可能反映偶然”相反，第三、四项明显与常识和原文矛盾。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Science is unreliable because its results are always uncertain
Publishing only successes is the best way to preserve confidence
A record limited to successes weakens a field's ability to test itself
Failures have little to do with scientific progress
questions.explain: 末段说科学之所以有效，是因为错误最终能被发现，而这需要把失败也记录在案；只发表胜利的领域会慢慢失去自我检验的能力，故选第三项。第一项误读“结果并非总是正确”，第二、四项与原文相反。

items.title: Why Small Public Spaces Matter
items.passage:
City planners once paid most attention to large parks and grand squares. These places are important, but they are not the whole story. A small public space at the end of a street can matter just as much to the people who live nearby. A few benches, a little shade, and a place to sit can turn an empty corner into a spot where neighbors meet.

Small spaces work best when they are easy to reach. Most people will not walk far for a short rest, so a tiny garden near a bus stop may be used more often than a large park across town. Older residents, parents with young children, and workers on a lunch break all benefit from places that fit easily into their day.

Comfort is a practical matter. Shade in summer, shelter from rain, and seats at the right height make a space usable across the seasons. Lighting matters too, because a place that feels pleasant in daylight may feel unsafe after dark. Good design is therefore less about costly statues than about small decisions that show someone has thought about how people will sit and wait.

Such spaces also support community life. When people see the same faces regularly, they begin to recognize one another, and that recognition can make a neighborhood feel more friendly and safer. This does not happen automatically; a space must be cared for, and it helps if local people have some say in how it is managed.

The lesson is simple. Cities often measure their success by large projects, but daily life is shaped mostly by small ones. A bench in the right place costs little and is used every day. Paying attention to these modest spaces is one of the least dramatic ways to improve urban life.

questions.q: What does the author say about large parks and squares?
options: They are unimportant compared with small gardens
They are important, but they are not the whole story
They should be replaced by seats at bus stops
They are used mainly by visitors from other cities
questions.explain: 首段承认大公园很重要，但“并非全部”，小型公共空间同样重要，故选第二项。第一项贬低了大公园的作用，第三项文中无此建议，第四项未提及。

questions.q: Why may a tiny garden near a bus stop be used more often than a large park?
options: It is usually cleaner and more beautiful
It offers more sports facilities
It fits easily into people's daily routes
It is open for longer hours
questions.explain: 第二段说人们不会为短暂休息走很远，因此靠近公交站的小花园比城另一头的大公园更常被使用，即它融入日常路线，故选第三项。其余三项文中均未提及。

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, what matters most in the design of small spaces?
options: Practical comfort such as shade, seating, and lighting
Expensive statues in the center
Very large fountains and pools
Tall buildings around the space
questions.explain: 第三段强调遮阴、避雨、合适高度的座椅与照明，并说好设计“不在于昂贵的雕像”，故选第一项。第二项被原文否定，第三、四项无据。

questions.q: The word "modest" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: expensive to build
crowded and noisy
famous among planners
small in scale and not impressive
questions.explain: 本段与“大型项目”对比，说长椅成本低却每天被使用，故 modest 指“规模小、不起眼”，与第四项相符。其余三项与上下文相反或无关。

questions.q: What can be inferred about community life in small spaces?
options: It develops automatically once a space is built
It depends entirely on large public budgets
It grows when people meet regularly and have some control over the space
It mainly benefits older residents
questions.explain: 第四段说熟悉的面孔带来相互识别，使社区更友好安全，但强调这“不会自动发生”，需要维护并让本地人参与管理，故选第三项。第一项被原文否定，第二项与“成本低”相反，第四项缩小了受益人群。

items.title: The Price of Speed in News
items.passage:
News used to arrive with delay. A report would be checked, edited, printed or broadcast, and only then reach its audience. The delay was often frustrating, but it had a use: it created a space in which errors could be caught. Today that space has narrowed, and in some cases it has disappeared. The first version of a story may reach readers within moments of an event, long before anyone has had time to confirm what happened.

Speed is not in itself a fault. In a crisis, timely information can save lives, and audiences reasonably expect to hear about important events quickly. The difficulty is that speed and accuracy pull in different directions. Verification takes time: a claim must be traced to a source, a document checked, a photograph examined. Every one of those steps can be skipped, and skipping them is invisible to the reader.

Competition sharpens the temptation. When attention is scarce, being first attracts readers, and a correction rarely travels as far as the original error. Journalists know this, which is why many newsrooms have built habits that protect the checking process: two sources for a serious claim, a separate editor to review a sensitive story, and clear rules about what may be published on the basis of a single message.

The audience has a part to play as well. Readers who reward speed with clicks and shares encourage the behavior they complain about. Slower, explanatory journalism is expensive to produce and easy to ignore, yet it is often what people claim to want. There is a mismatch between what audiences say they value and what their attention actually supports.

None of this is an argument for sluggishness. It is an argument for making the trade-off explicit. A newsroom that says "we will be quick, but we will not publish an unverified claim" is making a promise that can be judged. Speed with visible limits is more honest than speed presented as accuracy.

questions.q: What can be inferred about delay in news reporting in the past?
options: It was always harmful to the public
It made newspapers less interesting to read
It provided a chance to catch errors before publication
It was created mainly by government rules
questions.explain: 首段说过去的延迟虽有不便，却“有用处”：它创造了一个可以抓出错误的空间，故选第三项。第一项与原文相反，第二、四项无据。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what makes verification difficult?
options: It takes time, and its steps can be skipped without readers noticing
It requires technology that most newsrooms lack
It is impossible to carry out during a crisis
It slows down the printing of newspapers
questions.explain: 第二段说核实时要追溯来源、查文件、看照片，每一步都可被跳过且读者看不见，故第一项正确。第二项无据，第三项只涉及危机中的时效，第四项与“印刷”无关。

questions.q: Which practice does the passage mention as protecting accuracy?
options: Publishing a story on the basis of a single message
Removing corrections after a story is updated
Sharing every rumor as soon as it appears
Requiring two sources for a serious claim
questions.explain: 第三段列举新闻编辑室的核查习惯：重大指控要有两个来源、敏感报道需独立编辑复核等，故选第四项。第一项恰是规则要约束的做法，第二、三项与核查精神相反。

questions.q: The word "sluggishness" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: carelessness about facts
slowness in reporting
dishonesty toward readers
silence about mistakes
questions.explain: 末段开头澄清作者并非主张新闻“迟缓”，而是主张把取舍讲清楚，故该词指“缓慢”。第一、三、四项分别指粗心、不诚实与沉默，均非该词含义。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about audience behavior?
options: Readers always prefer slower, explanatory journalism
Clicks and shares have no effect on newsroom choices
What readers reward with attention may conflict with what they say they value
Audiences are unable to judge whether a report is accurate
questions.explain: 第四段指出读者用点击和分享奖励速度，反而鼓励了他们所抱怨的做法，说明“口头上重视的”与“注意力实际支持的”存在错位，故选第三项。第一项与“容易忽视深度报道”矛盾，第二项与“竞争加剧诱惑”相反，第四项过度绝对。

items.title: The Power of Small Habits
items.passage:
People who try to change a habit often begin with a large promise. They plan to exercise every morning, read more, or stop checking a phone at night. Such resolutions express genuine intention, yet many collapse within weeks. The failure is usually not a lack of willpower. It is more often a mismatch between the size of the plan and the ordinary conditions of daily life.

Research on habits suggests that repetition in a stable context is what makes behavior automatic. A habit is not merely a decision repeated; it becomes linked to a cue, such as a time of day, a place, or an action that comes before it. Once the link is strong, the behavior can unfold with little conscious effort. This is why so much advice focuses on designing cues rather than on summoning motivation.

Small steps have an advantage here. A modest action is easy to repeat, and repetition is what builds the link. Someone who intends to walk for a few minutes after lunch is more likely to do it consistently than someone who plans an hour at a gym. Consistency, in turn, produces the sense of identity that sustains habits: people who see themselves as someone who walks tend to keep walking.

The environment can quietly help or hinder. Leaving a book where it will be seen, or placing shoes by the door, reduces the effort required at the moment of decision. Conversely, a habit that depends on constant self-control is fragile, because attention and energy vary from day to day. Relying on willpower alone is a plan with a single point of failure.

Setbacks are normal and need not end a habit. The useful response is to resume quickly rather than to treat a missed day as proof of failure. A habit is better understood as a path that is followed most of the time, not as a perfect record. This gentler standard is easier to live with, and therefore easier to maintain.

questions.q: Why do many resolutions fail, according to the author?
options: The plans are too large for the ordinary conditions of daily life
People today lack willpower almost completely
Habits cannot really be changed once they are formed
People expect results too slowly to stay interested
questions.explain: 首段明确说失败通常不是意志力不足，而是计划规模与日常生活条件不匹配，故选第一项。第二项被作者否定，第三项过于绝对，第四项文中未提。

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, what makes behavior automatic?
options: Strong motivation at the start
Occasional rewards after success
Repeated action linked to a stable cue
Competition with other people
questions.explain: 第二段说在稳定情境中重复才会使行为自动化，行为与时间、地点等线索建立联系，故选第三项。第一项恰是作者认为不够的观点，第二、四项文中未提。

questions.q: The word "fragile" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: long-lasting and stable
easily disturbed and likely to break down
expensive to maintain
rarely noticed by other people
questions.explain: 本句说依赖持续自控的习惯是 fragile 的，因为注意力与精力每天都不同，故指“脆弱、容易被打断”。第一项与语义相反，第三、四项与语境无关。

questions.q: Why does the author mention placing shoes by the door?
options: To show that exercise requires special equipment
To suggest that tidy homes support healthy living
To warn readers against relying on self-control
To illustrate how reducing effort at decision time helps a habit
questions.explain: 第四段用“把书放在显眼处、把鞋放在门口”说明减少决策时刻的阻力有助于习惯，故选第四项。第一项并非举例目的，第二项文中未提整洁，第三项虽有相关意思但举例本身意在“减少阻力”。

questions.q: What does the author recommend after a missed day?
options: Start again with a much larger goal
Treat the miss as proof that the habit is impossible
Resume quickly rather than demand a perfect record
Abandon the habit and choose a different one
questions.explain: 末段说应尽快恢复，而不是把漏掉的一天当作失败的证据，故选第三项。第一项与“小步更易重复”相反，第二、四项都与作者“挫折很正常”的态度矛盾。

items.title: Cooking as a Life Skill
items.passage:
Cooking at home has become less common in many households. Long working hours, cheap prepared meals, and busy evenings all make it easier to buy food than to prepare it. There is nothing wrong with an occasional ready meal. But when cooking disappears from daily life altogether, people lose more than a little free time. They lose a skill that supports health, budget, and independence.

The health argument is simple. When you cook, you decide how much salt, sugar, and oil goes into a dish. You also decide the size of the portion. Restaurant and packaged food is not automatically unhealthy, but it is usually designed to be appealing, which often means richer and saltier than a person would make at home. Cooking is not a guarantee of good eating, but it gives you choices.

Cost is another reason. A simple meal made from basic ingredients is often cheaper than a takeaway meal, especially when it is shared. This does not mean that everyone should buy the same food. Fresh vegetables, beans, rice, eggs, and frozen produce can all form the base of affordable meals, and shopping with a plan reduces waste. Small habits, such as cooking a larger amount and keeping half for the next day, make the effort more practical.

Perhaps most importantly, cooking builds confidence. Someone who can prepare a few reliable dishes is less dependent on other people and on opening hours. This is useful in many situations: when money is short, when the shops are shut, or when someone simply wants to eat well. Learning three or four simple dishes is a good start. Skill grows with use, and the result is a practical kind of freedom.

questions.q: What does the author say about ready meals?
options: They should be completely banned from the home
They are always unhealthy and should be avoided
An occasional one is fine, but relying on them costs valuable skills
They are usually cheaper than cooking at home
questions.explain: 首段说偶尔吃一顿现成餐并无问题，但若烹饪从生活中完全消失，人失去的是健康、预算与独立所需的一项技能，故选第三项。第一、二项过于绝对，第四项与第三段“家常菜常更便宜”相反。

questions.q: What is one health benefit of cooking at home?
options: It removes all sugar from a meal
You control salt, sugar, oil, and portion size
It guarantees a perfectly balanced diet
It proves that restaurant food is always unhealthy
questions.explain: 第二段说下厨时由你决定盐、糖、油的用量与份量，故选第二项。第一项“all”过度，第三项与“不能保证吃得健康”相反，第四项是原文明确否认的说法。

questions.q: Which suggestion about affordable cooking is made in the passage?
options: Plan your shopping and cook larger amounts to use later
Buy only fresh vegetables and never frozen food
Avoid beans and rice because they are expensive
Stop eating out but never cook at home
questions.explain: 第三段建议带着计划购物以减少浪费，并提到一次多做一些留到次日，故选第一项。第二项与“冷冻食材也可以”矛盾，第三项与“豆类米饭可作基础”相反，第四项自相矛盾。

questions.q: The word "reliable" in paragraph 4 most probably means
options: expensive to prepare
quick to cook
new and unusual
dependable and known to work
questions.explain: 此处说会做几道“靠得住”的菜的人更能自立，故 reliable 指“可靠、行之有效”，与第四项相符。第二项看似相关，但作者强调的是稳定可靠而非速度；其余两项无关。

questions.q: What can be inferred from the last paragraph?
options: Cooking is a talent that people are born with
Only professional chefs can cook well
Confidence grows from learning a few dishes and practising
Cooking is useful only when money is short
questions.explain: 末段说学会三四道简单菜是好的开始，“技能随使用而增长”，故可推知信心来自学习与练习。第一、二项与“技能可以学习”相反，第四项缩小了烹饪的用处。

items.title: Making the Bus Feel Reliable
items.passage:
People often talk about public transport as a matter of vehicles: more buses, newer trains, extra routes. These things matter, but they are not what decides whether a service feels dependable. A journey that is predictable is easy to plan. A journey that may take much longer than expected is difficult to build a day around, even if the average travel time is short.

Reliability begins with information. Riders need to know not only when a bus is due but whether that promise can be trusted. Clear signs, simple apps, and announcements in stations help, but the information must be accurate. A screen that confidently shows a bus which is not coming may be worse than no screen at all, because it teaches people to stop planning and start waiting.

The route itself also shapes the experience. A service that goes everywhere is convenient in theory, but a long, winding route is slow and easy to delay. Simpler lines with frequent vehicles and easy changes often serve passengers better, even if a few people must walk a little farther. Comfort is part of reliability too: a crowded vehicle that passes waiting passengers is, from their point of view, a failure.

The final factor is trust. If problems are explained honestly, riders tolerate them more easily. Silence, by contrast, fills the gap with suspicion. A transport system that admits a delay, offers an alternative, and keeps talking to passengers builds a reputation for honesty even on a bad day. That reputation is valuable, because it encourages people to try the service again.

None of these ideas requires a new railway. Many improvements involve better information, clearer routes, and more honest communication. They are unglamorous, but they address what travelers actually experience. A network becomes reliable not only when it moves vehicles, but when it lets people plan with confidence.

questions.q: What do people often think public transport mainly needs?
options: More accurate information for passengers
More vehicles, newer trains, and extra routes
Cheaper tickets and longer opening hours
Better communication during delays
questions.explain: 首段说人们常把公共交通看作车辆问题：更多公交、更新的列车、更多线路，故选第二项。第一、四项是作者后文提出的重点，而非“人们常认为”的内容，第三项文中未提。

questions.q: Why can inaccurate information be worse than no information at all?
options: It costs the transport company a lot of money
It makes drivers and staff angry
It wastes electricity in stations
It teaches people to stop planning and simply wait
questions.explain: 第二段说屏幕 confidently 显示一辆不会来的车，可能比没有屏幕更糟，因为这会让人放弃计划、只是干等，故选第四项。其余三项文中均未提及。

questions.q: What does the author suggest about simple, frequent lines?
options: They can serve passengers better even if some people walk farther
They are always unpopular with local residents
They increase delays on long routes
They should be replaced by routes that go everywhere
questions.explain: 第三段说站点更少、班次更密的简单线路往往更方便，即使少数人要多走一点路，故选第一项。第二项与“往往更好地服务乘客”相反，第三项无据，第四项与作者对“处处都到”的批评矛盾。

questions.q: The word "unglamorous" in paragraph 5 most probably means
options: very costly to build
unusual and experimental
not exciting or impressive
dangerous for passengers
questions.explain: 末段说这些改进“不需要新建铁路”，虽不引人注目，却直接改善乘客体验，故指“不起眼、不光鲜”。第一、二、四项与语境不符。

questions.q: What can be inferred about trust in public transport?
options: It is impossible to build once a service is delayed
It depends only on buying new vehicles
It declines whenever information is accurate
Honest communication about problems helps to build it
questions.explain: 第四段说如实解释问题，乘客更容易接受，承认延误并提供替代方案的系统即便在糟糕的日子也能建立诚实的名声，故选第四项。第一项过于绝对，第二项与全文主旨相反，第三项与“准确信息有帮助”矛盾。

items.title: Meetings on the Move
items.passage:
Ask a group of office workers to describe their most {{1}} meetings and few will mention a conference room. The ones they remember tend to be conversations that happened while moving: on a walk to a nearby cafe or around a city block. That observation has led some managers to {{2}} the traditional seated discussion with a walking meeting, in which colleagues talk side by side rather than facing each other across a table.

Supporters insist the change is more than a fashion. Walking gives the body a steady rhythm, and that rhythm appears to {{3}} the grip of the usual workplace routine. Ideas that might have been ignored are more likely to be voiced. Because nobody is typing, the exchange becomes more {{4}}: people listen, pause, and answer in full sentences instead of firing off quick replies.

The arrangement also shifts the balance of power. In a conference room whoever sits at the head of the table tends to dominate, but outdoors that hierarchy {{5}}. Quieter members find it easier to {{6}} to the discussion, and a junior employee may speak as freely as a director. Difficult news, some say, is delivered more honestly on a footpath.

The method is not suitable for everything. A {{7}} budget needs a spreadsheet, and a complex plan needs diagrams that nobody can {{8}} while crossing a street. Weather is another {{9}} consideration, and long routes may leave out colleagues with {{10}} mobility. Experienced organisers therefore keep walks short, choose flat paths, and reserve the format for informal thinking. Used with care, a walk can turn a dull update into a conversation.

blanks.explain: 空格修饰 meetings，后文“the ones they remember”提示是“令人难忘的”，故填 memorable；hostile、fragile 与语境不符。
replace A with B 表示“用 B 取代 A”，与后面的 with a walking meeting 呼应；postpone、borrow、abandon 都不能构成该搭配。
appear to 后接动词原形，loosen the grip of... 意为“放松……的束缚”；postpone、borrow 等无法与 the grip 搭配。
because nobody is typing 以及人们认真倾听、完整作答，说明交流更“坦率”，candid 符合；hostile 与前后语气相反。
主语 hierarchy 为第三人称单数，dissolve 表示“（等级差别）消失”，语法与语义都成立；其余动词不合。
contribute to 表示“参与、对……有所贡献”；postpone、borrow 等不能接 to，abandon 语义也不合。
修饰 budget，指“详尽的预算”，需要形容词；hostile、fragile 语义不合。
sketch diagrams 意为“画示意图”，与“过马路时无法画图”的语境相符；borrow、abandon 不合。
practical consideration 指“实际层面的考虑”，天气和路线都属于实际因素；fragile 等不合。
limited mobility 是固定搭配，意为“行动不便”，与 long routes 的顾虑一致；hostile、fragile 不合。

items.title: Reading Aloud, Again
items.passage:
Most reading is silent and {{1}}: one person alone with a page. Reading aloud reverses that arrangement. It turns a private act into a performance with an {{2}}, and it slows the eye down to the speed of the voice. Teachers have long used the practice in classrooms, but adults rarely return to it once school ends. That is a pity, because reading to another person exercises skills that silent reading never touches.

The first is how words sound. A reader who has only met a word on the page may {{3}} before it, unsure how to {{4}} it; saying it out loud exposes the gap and, with practice, closes it. The second is attention to {{5}} and pace. A sentence read aloud has to be breathed, and punctuation becomes a set of instructions: stop here, lift there, slow down. The result is often more {{6}} than the same sentence read in silence, because the ear catches effects the eye skips.

There is also a social benefit. Listening to a story is one of the oldest forms of {{7}} entertainment, and it builds {{8}} between people in a way that scrolling alone does not. Libraries and community groups have begun to host reading evenings for exactly this reason, and participants report that they {{9}} far more of a text they have heard than of one they have merely scanned.

None of this requires talent. Reading aloud is a skill, not a {{10}}, and a short pause or a stumbled name matters far less than the willingness to try.

items.title: The Repair Habit
items.passage:
Not long ago, a broken toaster usually meant a trip to the bin. Today a growing number of people are choosing to {{1}} that habit and fix things instead. Repair cafes, where neighbours bring broken objects and fix them together, have appeared in many towns, and online forums offer step-by-step advice for almost any item.

The appeal is partly financial. A new appliance costs far more than a spare part, and mending is usually more {{2}} than buying another. But money is not the whole story. Many visitors say they come to learn a {{3}} their grandparents took for granted, or to spend time with people who enjoy taking things apart.

The social side matters as much as the technical one. Experienced {{4}} sit at long tables with toolboxes open, and a nervous owner can find {{5}} from someone who has fixed the same fault. Beginners often arrive convinced that they are useless with their hands; a few hours later they leave more {{6}} and eager to try another job.

Repair culture also changes how people shop. Once you have opened a machine and seen how it is built, you look for products that are {{7}} rather than sealed shut, and you become less willing to {{8}} a device that still has years of use. Manufacturers notice this: some now publish manuals and sell parts directly to customers, a policy that would have seemed odd a generation ago.

None of this will {{9}} the problem of electronic waste alone. But every object kept in use is one that does not reach the bin, and the habit of mending is {{10}} in a world of limited resources.

items.title: Museums Beyond the Glass Case
items.passage:
For generations the museum visit followed a simple rule: look, but do not touch. Objects sat behind glass, labels supplied dates, and visitors moved through rooms in silence. That model still suits many collections, yet it excludes anyone who cannot see well and leaves most people with only a faint impression of the past.

Designers have begun to {{1}} the experience. Some galleries now provide {{2}} copies of sculptures that visitors may handle, with labels in larger print and plain language. Others use sound: a recording of a workshop or the murmur of a market can {{3}} a scene more vividly than text.

The change is not only about disability. Curators have found that a multi-sensory room holds school groups far longer than a case of objects, and that families stay until closing. When a visitor can lift a replica sword or smell the resin used in a boat, the past becomes something like a memory.

Critics warn that replicas may {{4}} real objects in the minds of visitors, and that a museum should not {{5}} scholarship for novelty. Curators answer that the two goals are not in {{6}}. A careful reconstruction, they argue, draws attention to the original rather than {{7}} its importance. Many institutions now label replicas clearly and invite visitors to compare the copy with the genuine item.

The biggest {{8}} is training. Front-of-house staff need time to {{9}} new formats, and small museums often lack the money to build them. Still, the principle is hard to {{10}}: a collection that few people can fully experience serves the public less well than one that welcomes everybody.

items.title: Birdsong in the City
items.passage:
Early in the morning, before the streets fill, a city can sound almost like a forest. Blackbirds, sparrows, and gulls sing from rooftops and plane trees, and for a few minutes the {{1}} of traffic is drowned out. City dwellers who notice this are often surprised, because the common view is that wildlife belongs to the countryside.

The truth is more interesting. Cities support fewer species than forests, but the birds that do live there are often remarkably {{2}}. Some have learned to sing at a higher pitch so that their songs can be heard above low engine {{3}}. Others have shifted the hours of their dawn chorus, starting earlier when the background is quieter. Such adjustments happen over decades rather than overnight, yet they show how quickly animals can {{4}} to an artificial environment.

For humans the benefits run the other way. Many office workers and hospital patients say that a view of greenery, or even a recording of birdsong, can {{5}} recovery and calm the nerves. This may explain why urban planners now {{6}} parks and green roofs not as decoration but as public health measures.

None of this happens by accident. A city that {{7}} nature needs space for insects, water for drinking, and trees old enough to shelter nests. It also needs residents who will {{8}} the racket their own machinery makes. Several councils have placed a {{9}} on building work during the breeding season, and some have dimmed street lights to help birds rest.

Such measures are cheap compared with the cost of a city that has {{10}} its birds, where the only sound is the traffic that drove them away.

items.title: Gardens Above the Street
items.passage:
Look down on a modern city from a high window and you will see a grey landscape of roofs. Look again in a few years and some of those roofs may have turned green. Rooftop gardens, once a novelty on expensive apartment blocks, are spreading to schools, offices, and public housing, and they are changing the way cities {{1}} heat, water, and food.

The environmental case is easy to {{2}}. A layer of soil and plants absorbs sunlight that would otherwise be {{3}} by concrete, so the building below stays cooler in summer. The plants also slow rainwater, which {{4}} the pressure on drains during storms. In dense neighbourhoods where ground space is scarce, a roof may be the only {{5}} place to grow vegetables.

The social case is less obvious but just as {{6}}. A shared garden gives neighbours a reason to talk, and a school roof can become an outdoor classroom where children learn where food comes from. Tenants who have never met may find themselves {{7}} tomatoes together on a Saturday morning.

Rooftop gardens are not {{8}}, however. The structure must carry the weight of wet soil, the waterproofing must be perfect, and someone must water the plants in dry spells. Costs can {{9}} quickly, and a poorly planned garden may be abandoned within a season.

Cities that have made the gardens work usually started small. A single pilot roof allowed engineers to test the load, gardeners to learn which plants {{10}} the wind, and residents to see the benefit for themselves. Success then spread by example rather than by rule.

items.title: Letters in the Drawer
items.passage:
A handwritten letter arrives slowly. It may take days to reach its reader, and its paper carries the marks of a particular day: a smudge, a crossed-out word, a change of pen. In an age of {{1}} messages, that slowness looks like a fault. Yet people who write letters by hand describe the practice as a form of {{2}} that no screen can imitate.

The difference begins with time. Typing a message encourages a quick reply, while writing by hand forces the writer to {{3}} each sentence before it is committed to paper. The hand moves more slowly than the mind, and that gap gives the writer room to {{4}} what is worth saying. Many letter writers say their real thoughts appear only after the second page.

A letter also lasts. Emails pile up in an inbox and are rarely read twice, whereas a letter can be kept in a drawer for years. Grandchildren may one day {{5}} a bundle of envelopes and learn what their grandparents were like as young people. In this sense, a letter is less a message than a small {{6}} of a life.

Handwriting itself carries meaning. A hasty scrawl suggests impatience; a careful loop suggests care. None of this can be conveyed by a standard font, however {{7}} the design. The reader hears a voice even though nothing is spoken.

None of this means that digital messages are {{8}}. They are simply different tools, suited to different tasks. The {{9}} is to keep both: a quick note to confirm a meeting, and, now and then, a letter that shows someone you were willing to spend an {{10}} on them.

items.title: The Usefulness of Boredom
items.passage:
Reach for a phone whenever a queue forms or a train stops in a tunnel, and you will rarely be bored. That reflex has become so {{1}} that many people cannot remember the last time they sat with nothing to do. The result may be a quiet loss of something valuable.

Boredom has a bad name, and for good reason: nobody enjoys the restless feeling of a dull afternoon. Yet boredom is also a signal. It tells us that the current activity is not {{2}} us, and it pushes us to look for something better. In that sense it works like pain, which we dislike but which keeps us from harm.

The trouble is that we now treat every gap in the day as a problem to be {{3}}. A moment of inactivity is filled with a video, a game, or a stream of messages. Convenient as this is, it may {{4}} the mind's habit of wandering. When the brain is not occupied by a task, it {{5}} to connect ideas that seemed unrelated, and these connections are the raw material of {{6}}.

Psychologists who study attention suggest a simple experiment. Leave the phone in another room for an hour and see what happens. The first ten minutes may feel {{7}}. Then the mind begins to drift, and the drift is not a failure; it is the mind exercising. People who {{8}} this practice often report that they notice details around them and arrive at solutions they had been {{9}} for days.

None of this argues for a duller life. It argues for a life with more {{10}} between the interesting parts.

blanks.explain: so automatic 指掏手机已变成“下意识的”反应，与 cannot remember the last time 呼应；sudden 不合。

items.title: The Recycling Club
items.passage:
At the start of the school year, a group of students noticed something simple. Every lunchtime, the bins outside the dining hall were filled with paper cups, plastic bottles, and half-eaten sandwiches. The students decided to start a recycling club, and within a term it had changed the habits of the whole school.

The first step was to {{1}} what was actually being thrown away. For a week, members wore gloves and sorted the rubbish from one bin into different boxes. The results were {{2}}: more than half of it could have been reused or recycled. The club put the boxes in the hall so that everyone could see them, and the {{3}} made a stronger impression than any poster.

Next came the practical part. The club asked the school to put separate bins in every corridor and to {{4}} the staff about what belonged where. They also wrote a short guide and {{5}} it to each classroom. Some teachers were {{6}} at first, because the new system took time, but most agreed once they saw how much waste had {{7}}.

The club did not stop at lunchtime. Members visited younger classes to talk about the {{8}} of throwing everything into one bin, and they organised a day when students brought old books and clothes to school for others to take home. The event was so {{9}} that the school has decided to hold it twice a year.

What began as a small idea has become part of the timetable. The students say the biggest {{10}} is not money but patience: habits change slowly, and a club needs members who will keep going when the first excitement fades.

items.title: A Town Learns to Cycle
items.passage:
Ten years ago, most people in this town drove to work, even when the journey was only a few minutes long. Today the picture looks different. A new cycle path runs beside the river, the office car park is half empty, and warm mornings bring bicycles into town. The change did not happen by itself.

The council began by making cycling safer. It {{1}} the busiest street so that cars had less space and bikes had a lane. It also added a bridge over the ring road, which {{2}} the most dangerous part of the journey. At first, shop owners were {{3}} that fewer parking spaces would mean fewer customers, but the opposite proved true: cyclists stopped more often than drivers.

Employers helped as well. Several offices installed showers and secure racks, and a few now {{4}} staff a small sum for every day they cycle. One manager explained that cyclists arrive more {{5}} and take fewer sick days, so the money is well spent.

Not everyone is {{6}} that cycling is safe, of course. Older residents and parents of young children still find the traffic frightening, and the town has not yet {{7}} enough pavements. The council plans to spend the next year {{8}} the gaps in the network, starting near schools.

What has changed most is how people think about cyclists. Riders were once seen as a small group in special clothing; now they are ordinary people carrying shopping or heading to work. That change in {{9}} may be as important as the new path. A town that once laughed at cycling now {{10}} it as a normal way to travel.

items.title: A Notebook by the Bed
items.passage:
Many people buy a notebook in January, write in it for a week, and then leave it in a drawer. Keeping a diary sounds easy, but it asks for a habit that most of us never build. Those who do keep one often say the same thing: the value comes not from style but from {{1}}.

A diary does not need to be a work of art. You can {{2}} down a few lines about what you ate, who you met, or how you felt. The point is to {{3}} the day before it disappears. Memory is {{4}}, and small details that seem unimportant today may be the ones you most want to read in ten years.

There are practical {{5}}, too. Writing about a worry can make it smaller, because putting it into words {{6}} you to see its shape. Some doctors even suggest a diary for people who find it hard to sleep, since a page of notes can {{7}} the mind for rest.

The habit is easier to keep if you make it {{8}}. Keep the notebook beside your bed, choose a fixed time, and do not worry about grammar. If you miss a day, simply start again; nobody is marking your work. It also pays to write in the same {{9}} each time, so that opening the notebook becomes a signal that the day is over.

After a year, the reward is clear. You will have a record of ordinary life that no photograph can {{10}}, and you may understand yourself a little better than when you began.

items.title: Saturday at the Shelter
items.passage:
Every Saturday morning, a small group of people gathers at the animal shelter on the edge of town. They are not staff. They are {{1}}, and they come to walk dogs, clean cages, and spend time with cats that have been waiting a long time for a home.

Most of them started with a simple wish to help, and discovered that the work {{2}} more than it takes. Dogs that are walked regularly become {{3}} and easier to adopt. Cats that are touched every day learn to trust people again. A helper who arrives feeling tired often leaves feeling {{4}}, because the animals do not care about the problems waiting at home.

The shelter's manager says the helpers are {{5}} to its survival. The budget covers food and medical care, but there is never enough money for extra staff. Without people who {{6}} their free time, many animals would spend whole days alone.

Volunteering is not always {{7}}. Some animals are frightened, some are sick, and a few cannot be adopted at all. New helpers are trained to {{8}} the rules: wash your hands, watch your fingers, and never open a cage without asking. It can be {{9}} at first, but most people find the routine satisfying.

The shelter also asks its helpers to {{10}} the message that an animal is a long-term responsibility. A puppy given as a gift may be abandoned by winter. If more people understood that, fewer dogs would be waiting on a Saturday morning.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Buying used goods once carried a faint smell of hardship. Today the same act is presented as clever, thrifty and even stylish. Influential voices online show off furniture rescued from skips and coats found in charity shops, and their audiences copy the behaviour. The shift is partly economic and partly cultural: people want their purchases to say something about their values as well as their taste. Parents who once hid a second-hand purchase now mention it proudly. As a result, a market that was once hidden at the edge of town has moved into the mainstream.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The environmental argument is straightforward. Every object that changes hands a second time is an object that does not have to be manufactured, shipped and eventually buried. That saves materials, energy and space in landfill. Campaigners point out that the greenest item is usually the one already in existence, and that buying nothing new is more effective than buying something labelled sustainable. For a generation worried about waste, this logic is difficult to argue with. The calculation differs from person to person, but the direction is the same.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Second-hand shopping requires a different kind of attention. A buyer cannot assume that a coat has been cleaned or that a chair has all its legs. Photographs may hide stains, and a description that sounds enthusiastic may omit a fault. Experienced shoppers inspect seams, ask about measurements and request extra images before they commit. They also learn to walk away from a bargain that will cost more to repair than to replace. A little patience saves both money and disappointment.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Online platforms have solved the trust problem in a simple way: they let strangers rate each other. A seller with hundreds of positive reviews is unlikely to risk a bad one for a small gain, and buyers who feel cheated can warn others. Some sites hold the payment until the item arrives, which removes the fear of paying for nothing. These small mechanisms have made it normal to send money to somebody you have never met. Reputation, in other words, has replaced the handshake.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: For many sellers the motivation is not money but space. A flat fills up with clothes that no longer fit and gadgets that were used twice, and throwing them away feels wasteful. Listing an item takes minutes, and the buyer often collects it from the doorstep. The result is a home that feels lighter and a small sum that appears in the bank. Sellers describe the process as a form of tidying that pays for itself. Some describe selling as a way of learning what they never use.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Older objects have an advantage that new ones often lack. Furniture built decades ago was frequently made from solid wood and designed to be mended, while a cheap modern equivalent may be glued together and impossible to repair. Collectors seek out such pieces for their materials and their character, and some manufacturers have noticed, reissuing classic designs or emphasising durability in their marketing. The appeal is not only nostalgia; it is also a judgement about quality that buyers can test with their hands.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The risks are real. Counterfeit goods, stolen bicycles and items that arrive broken are all part of the picture. Most platforms offer some protection, but a buyer who pays in cash on a doorstep has little recourse. Consumer groups advise meeting in public places, keeping a record of the conversation, and checking serial numbers where possible. They also warn that a price far below the market rate is usually a warning sign. Vigilance, rather than trust, is the price of a good bargain.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Retailers have responded not by fighting the trend but by joining it. Several chains now buy back worn clothing and resell it, and electronics shops offer trade-in credit against a new purchase. The motive is partly ethical and partly commercial: a customer who returns to sell is a customer who may also buy. For the shops, the second-hand section attracts people who would otherwise never enter the store. For them the used rail is less a threat than an extra shop window.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Clothing shows the pattern most clearly. Fashion cycles now move quickly, and garments are often worn a few times before losing their appeal. Resale gives them a second life and gives buyers a way to follow trends without paying full price. Some young shoppers build whole wardrobes from used items and treat the hunt as entertainment. Critics worry that this simply speeds up consumption rather than reducing it. The industry has noticed, and some labels now design clothes with resale in mind.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Lawmakers are beginning to catch up. Rules that once applied only to shops are being extended to individuals who sell regularly, and platforms are expected to check that goods are not stolen. Consumer protection bodies want the same guarantees for used products that new ones receive. Sellers complain about paperwork, but the direction of travel is clear: the second-hand market is no longer a private arrangement between neighbours. What was once a favour between friends is becoming a market with obligations.

statements.text: Buying second-hand is now treated as a smart and principled choice rather than a sign of poverty.
Choosing an object that already exists is greener than buying a new one marketed as sustainable.
Used goods demand close inspection because sellers may not mention every defect.
Reputation scores and delayed payment let strangers trade safely without meeting.
Many people sell mainly to clear space and feel better about their homes.
Well-made old furniture is prized because cheap modern versions cannot be repaired.
Shoppers are warned about unusually low prices and advised to keep evidence.
Established shops join resale because it brings in people who rarely visit.
Fast fashion drives resale while also raising doubts about total consumption.
Rules once aimed at businesses are being applied to frequent individual sellers.

items.title: Hiring for Skill, Not for Talk

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The traditional job interview is a conversation between strangers, and it is a poor predictor of how someone will actually work. Candidates who are charming and fluent often impress an interviewer without demonstrating any relevant ability, while quieter applicants with stronger skills may be overlooked. Employers have long known this, but the interview survived because it was cheap and familiar. Now that hiring is expensive and mistakes are visible, more companies are looking for evidence rather than impressions. The cost of a poor appointment is easier to notice than the weakness of the conversation that led to it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most direct alternative is a work sample. A designer is asked to redesign a page, an analyst to interpret a small dataset, and a customer service candidate to answer a set of realistic complaints. Because the task resembles the job, performance on it tells an employer something that no conversation can. Candidates generally prefer this too: a practical test feels fairer than being judged on small talk and a firm handshake. Employers also find that a task reveals how a person handles instructions and deadlines.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Practical hiring can widen the pool of applicants. A person without a degree may still write excellent code or manage a project calmly, and a test allows that ability to surface. Employers who drop formal qualification requirements often report a larger and more varied set of candidates. For workers who learned their trade outside universities, this is a rare route past a filter that would otherwise reject them before any human being reads their name. A test, unlike a degree, can be designed around the actual work rather than around a syllabus.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: There is a catch. A take-home task can amount to hours of unpaid work, and candidates with caring responsibilities cannot always spare an evening. Some firms have responded by keeping tasks short, paying a small fee, or running the exercise during a scheduled session. Without such safeguards, a method that looks objective may simply reward people with free time, which is a poor proxy for talent. The fairness of the process, not its sophistication, decides whether candidates trust it.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Skills-based hiring also changes how existing staff are treated. Instead of relying on job titles, an organisation can assess what employees can actually do and move them into roles where those abilities are needed. This is popular with workers who feel stuck in a department because their formal qualifications do not match a vacancy. It also helps employers fill gaps internally when the external market is thin. The result is a workforce that can be redeployed instead of replaced.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The approach only works if the people doing the assessing are trained. An untrained interviewer may favour a candidate who reminds them of themselves, or may mark an unusual but effective solution as wrong. Good practice includes agreeing in advance what a strong answer looks like, scoring independently, and comparing notes afterwards. None of this is complicated, but it does require time that many managers say they do not have. Consistency matters more than cleverness: two assessors should reach similar conclusions.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Smaller firms face a particular difficulty. Designing, running and marking a realistic task costs money, and a business with a handful of employees may not have anyone free to do it. Some have joined forces with local colleges or industry groups to share the burden, while others use standardised tests bought from specialist providers. The risk is that a cheaper test drifts away from the actual demands of the job. A test borrowed from another industry may measure skills the job never requires.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Assessment can also be gamed. Once candidates know what a test involves, coaching services appear, and the results start to measure preparation rather than ability. Companies defend themselves by changing tasks regularly and by observing how people work, not only what they produce. A candidate who has rehearsed an answer may still struggle when asked to explain a decision or to respond to an unexpected change. Honesty about the limits of testing is part of a credible process.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: Degrees have not become irrelevant, but their role is shifting. A qualification still signals persistence and a certain level of knowledge, yet it is increasingly treated as one piece of evidence among several. In fields where the technology changes quickly, a portfolio of recent work may say more than a certificate earned years ago. Employers who insist on a degree in such fields risk excluding exactly the people who keep their skills current. What a candidate has built recently may matter more than what they studied years ago.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The hardest abilities to assess are the ones that matter most in teams: listening, negotiating and noticing when a colleague is struggling. A written exercise cannot easily capture them, and a group task may reward loudness. The best employers combine methods, using tests for technical skill and structured conversations for behaviour, and they accept that no single instrument is decisive. Judgement remains part of hiring, however many tools are added. No method removes the need for judgement, only the need to rely on a single impression.

statements.text: Interviews tend to reward confidence and fluency instead of evidence of competence.
Tasks modelled on real duties reveal abilities that conversation cannot.
Assessment can open doors for candidates without conventional qualifications.
Unpaid tasks disadvantage people with limited time, so safeguards are needed.
Existing employees can be moved according to demonstrated ability rather than titles.
Evaluators must be trained and use consistent criteria to avoid personal bias.
Small employers may share or buy assessment tools, though relevance can suffer.
Predictable tests invite coaching, so results reveal preparation as much as ability.
A degree now counts as one signal among many, especially where skills date quickly.
Teamwork qualities resist simple testing, so firms combine several methods.

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Roads and railways cut the landscape into pieces. For an animal that needs a large territory, a motorway is not a line on a map but an impassable wall. Populations on one side become isolated, and over time they lose the genetic variety that helps them survive disease and climate stress. Fragmentation is a quieter threat than hunting or pollution, yet it may be the one that empties a forest of its larger inhabitants. The damage is done not by a single road but by the network that grows around it.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Engineers have responded with structures that let animals cross without meeting traffic. The best known are wide bridges covered with soil and planted with shrubs, which deer and foxes use without appearing to notice the road beneath. Underpasses serve smaller species, and tunnels built for drainage can be adapted for amphibians. Design matters: an opening that looks dark and narrow may be avoided even when it is perfectly safe. A crossing that animals refuse to use is an expensive decoration.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The evidence that such crossings work comes from cameras, footprints and tracking collars. Recordings show badgers, wild cats and even insects using the same routes night after night. Where a crossing has been placed badly, the data show that too, which allows the design to be corrected. Monitoring is unglamorous, but it turns a hopeful construction project into a measurable one. Without it, nobody can say whether the money was well spent.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Money and politics are the obvious obstacles. A wildlife bridge can cost as much as a small road, and the benefit is hard to demonstrate within a single political term. Supporters therefore emphasise the benefits to people: fewer collisions, safer journeys and, in some places, a tourist attraction.
